rv.q: It’s an affecting tale but not entirely bleak.
Yet Amit Sharma’s production, threaded through with folk song, has, for all its terrors, an element of fable – and of a modest, truthful piece of theatre blinking in the semi-commercial glare.
But in its determination to tell a neatly rounded story, it neglects other, less palatable, less familiar truths.
Yet often, sad to say, it’s the very goodness of the Amiris in this telling that works against a true sense of the horror of what they go through.
There’s a sheer moral clarity to its directness, even if it is inescapably flawed theatre.
I wish them well, but as entertainment, it's way too jolly for me.
The play is heartfelt and heartwarming, twice over.

Yet this theatrical retelling feels frustratingly underpowered and sadly overshadowed by the new stories emerging daily from a country that once more has proved that, for better or worse, it will always be a law unto itself.
I confess to tiring somewhat of the cutesier passages where things are told rather than shown and where we are informed rather unnecessarily that the tale on view “is about all of us”.
Charming, but ultimately middle-of-the-road verging on saccharine, The Boy With Two Hearts’ lack of depth is a real pity.

cn.t: Critics find this Afghan refugee family's true story emotionally moving but fault the production for oversimplified, unsubtle storytelling that doesn't fully do justice to the harrowing journey it depicts.
